Abstract
The Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) applications have been recognized as an advancement of the conventional wireless network 
that concentrates on incorporating processes and machines specifically for industrial applications. These Industrial applications 
frequently use centralized machine learning (ML) approaches not only to enhance their functionality but also to evaluate sensor 
data for a variety of purposes, including digitizing operations in manufacturers, forecasting maintenance requirements in industrial 
equipment, and detecting anomalies for security monitoring, they may adversely affect overall system performance due to high 
cost of computing power and privacy concerns, as so much data is stored on a cloud server. Federated Learning (FL) has emerged 
as a new benchmark for centralized ML methods. It sends models to user devices without transferring private data to third-party 
or central servers; it is one of the promising solutions to data leakage issues. This work introduces a comprehensive overview of 
the advancements, challenges, and future directions in FL adoption with edge devices. It covers security threats and mitigation 
strategies, emphasizing its categories, privacy and concerns, communication overhead obstacles, heterogeneity issues, aggrega-
tion techniques, and associated development tools. This review paper delves into FL-related topics, including system platforms, 
offering a comprehensive overview of best practice systems in real-world FL applications. To ensure security in IIoT applications, 
reviewing threats and mitigation strategies by integrating FL with state-of-the-art technologies such as blockchain, federated 
reinforcement learning, and federated meta-learning has been explored. Finally, the recent research is taking place to determine 
new future directions and opportunities for FL security defense mechanisms has been considered at the end of this review paper.

1  Introduction
The Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) enables the intercon-
nection of numerous sensors, devices, and machines within 
industrial environments, generating large volumes of data. 
Federated Learning (FL) provides a distributed and privacy-
preserving approach for training Machine Learning (ML) 
models on this data. Unlike traditional ML approaches that 
need data to be collected on a central server, FL allows data 
to remain on local devices and only sends model updates 
to the central server. Currently, most businesses cannot 
implement data-hungry AI services due to the lack of nec-
essary and sufficient data. Therefore, many businesses look 
for valuable data offered by commercial companies [1, 2]. 
Most data users possess personal information, such as travel 
history and health status. However, uploading unencrypted 
raw data to a Deep Learning (DL) server is uncertain. FL is 
a decentralized DL system that combines several clients to 
increase the efficacy of the FL model while ensuring data

There is a growing emphasis on research in FL, which 
recognizes the specific challenges and issues associated 
with FL, such as heterogeneity and security concerns related 
to the central server. To address these issues and further 
promote development, Blockchain technology [5] is being 
introduced as an alternative to the traditional central server 
used in FL. Blockchain is a distributed and immutable ledger 
involving digital records linked and secured through cryp-
tography. This technology ensures transparent information 
sharing among Blockchain participants, creating a secure 
environment for decentralized systems [6].
Integrating blockchain technology and FL presents a 
promising paradigm to enhance the security for advancing 
intelligent IIoT systems [7]. It can leverage the power of FL 
to enable localized model training on edge devices, ensuring 
data privacy and reducing the requirement for transmitting 
data to centralized servers through blockchain technology 
[8]. This integration empowers industrial systems to perform 
real-time analytics, predictive maintenance, and anomaly 
detection at the edge, minimizing latency and enhancing 
operational efficiency [1–4]. Furthermore, FL enables col-
laborative knowledge sharing among various industrial enti-
ties and allows collaborative learning from diverse datasets 
while preserving the privacy of sensitive data [9]. However, 
recent research has revealed that effective privacy protec-
tion techniques and attack mitigation methods are still 
bottlenecks. The requirement for more hardware resources 
may result in communication overhead, especially when 
many clients participate in their information. Moreover, the 
heterogeneity of IIoT devices and client data distribution 
leads to global model drift, and models trained by clients 
participating in federated tasks are often different. These 
challenges highlight the need for improvements in both FL 
and IIoT techniques. FL techniques have overcome numer-
ous limitations to find a way into various fields such as smart 
cities, edge computing, banking and assurance, smart health-
care, intrusion detection, and smart industrial applications 
[4, 10–20].
Vulnerabilities in smart healthcare can result in mis-
diagnoses, inappropriate medication use, and significant 
risks to human life. In IIoT devices, attacks may lead 
to financial losses and compromise sensitive informa-
tion. While various defense strategies, such as anomaly 
detection and secure aggregation protocols, are designed 
to counteract poisoning attacks [21]. This paper reviews 
aggregation techniques in FL, emphasizing their capacity 
to address the challenges associated with FL. Poisoning 
attacks occur when malicious clients alter local data or 
model updates, weakening system performance or gain-
ing unauthorized access. These attackers may introduce 
fraudulent data samples or manipulate model updates, 
leading to inaccurate results in the global model. The pri-
mary types of attacks include data poisoning, model poi-
soning, and backdoor attacks, all of which use falsified

2  The concept of FL
This section presents a general overview of FL categoriza-
tion based on the data distributions among multiple partici-
pants, the main challenges and limitations of FL followed 
by recent FL methodologies for optimization. Furthermore, 
it presents a comparison of recent techniques that seek to 
address the identified challenges (Fig. 2).
2.1  FL categorization
Based on the data distributions among multiple participants, 
FL can be categorized into three types: horizontal FL, verti-
cal FL, and federated transfer learning [20]. However, differ-
ent categorizations have been proposed based on how data is 
shared between diverse parties in the feature and sample ID 
spaces. To better illustrate this division, Figure 3 has been 
included, followed by a brief introduction to each category.

I.	 Horizontal FL: Horizontal Federated Learning 
(HFL) is a popular technique that is used in situa-
tions where there is a lot of overlap in data features 
among the users or when there are a limited number 
of individuals with similar data characteristics. HFL 
works by selecting components that share common 
characteristics as the participants but are distinct 
individuals, based on the dimension of the data. By 
combining the samples from the participants, HFL 
expands the training sample space, which leads to 
improved model accuracy and generalization. In this 
scenario, each device has a unique model, making 
it possible for independent predictions to be made 
during the training process. Regardless of any model 
loss, each user's privacy is preserved because they 
train their raw data centrally and only exchange local 
gradient parameters [1].
	 II.	 Vertical FL: In the case of Vertical Federated Learn-
ing (VFL), the scenario is opposite to HFL. The 
user overlap tends to be more significant in VFL 
than the overlap in data features. This implies that 
while there are more users in each dataset, there are 
fewer duplicated data features [24]. On the other 
hand, HFL concentrates on feature dimensions 
and segments accordingly. It aligns data based on 
common users and extracts groups of participants 
who had common characteristics for cooperative 
training but did not share all of them with similar 
users. Achieving this requires sample alignment 
of each participant's data utilized for training after 
first being used to collect repeated user data [25]. 
For instance, consider airlines and hotels. Although 
they hold distinct records of the same individual, 
encompassing flight and accommodation details, 
it is vital to maintain the security of this data. 
VFL addresses this concern through sample align-
ment and model encryption [26, 27]. This method 
ensures that during the training phase, other par-
ticipants cannot access each other's data and traits. 
Consequently, the global model can acquire data 
insights from all participants, without any compro-
mise to the model's integrity.
	 III.	 Federated Transfer Learning: It appears that the 
federated transfer learning (FTL) application sce-
nario is quite stringent, with a small and uniform 
user base, as well as standardized data sets. How-
ever, it's encouraging to see a strong emphasis on 
improving user satisfaction, particularly in areas like 
wearable healthcare devices [28]. HFL and VFL need 
users to have common features to construct a pow-
erful shared ML model [1, 25]. FTL is an effective 
methodology that can tackle challenges beyond the 
scope of current approaches. Transfer learning (TL) 
provides a practical solution by allowing information 
to be transferred from one domain to another. The 
basic concept of FTL is to take a pre-trained model 
from the source domain, which has a wealth of data, 
and use a few labeled target samples to fine-tune it 
based on data similarities [28–30]. Source domain 
tags are frequently utilized in various applications to 
estimate the correctness of tags in the target domain 
[29]. To better illustrate the diverse characteristics, 
collaboration mechanisms, challenges, and applica-
tion scenarios of HFL, VFL, and FTL, a comparative 
analysis is summarized in Table 1.

2.2  FL: challenges and solutions in IIoT
FL is a novel technology that offers significant benefits for 
IIoT applications, such as privacy preservation and distrib-
uted intelligence. However, the FL system still faces several 
challenges and limitations, which endanger its full potential 
in IIoT environments, including communication overhead, 
system and data heterogeneity, and security risks. Figure 4 
summarizes the integration between FL and IIoT and key 
challenges that will be further explored in the following 
sections along with existing research efforts and potential 
solutions.
I. High Communication Cost: FL faces many significant 
challenges, including high communication overheads that 
often exceed the computational cost. This is especially 
true when multiple IIoT devices send their model param-
eters to a central server. The substantial communication 
costs hinder the training efficiency of FL and limit its 
practical applications. The high communication overhead 
can overwhelm the network in bandwidth-constrained 
IIoT environments, such as smart cities or large indus-
trial automation. This can lead to latency, packet loss, 
and increased energy consumption. Researchers have pro-
posed three primary perspectives and various methods to 
tackle this challenge:
(a) FL Methodologies for optimization: Clients cre-
ate local models during the FL training procedure 
using optimization techniques like gradient descent 
(GD) and then send these models to the centrally 
located server for aggregation. It has been discov-
ered that improving local training iterations while 
decreasing global communication rounds improves 
the global model's convergence efficiency. The

Client Selection: In synchronous FL, the server 
waiting for model updates from every client may 
affect the reliability and effectiveness of the model. 
It's essential to have a good client selection scheme 
that considers these factors for optimal outcomes 
[35, 36]. Researchers have been studying and devel-
oping methods to tackle the challenge of select-
ing the most suitable clients for learning, includ-
ing filtering relevant updates to conserve network 
resources. The Scaffold technique [32] mitigates 
client drifting by utilizing a variance reduction strat-
egy. In predictive maintenance for the FL systems, 
Scaffold demonstrated faster convergence and better 
generalization. Nevertheless, it requires balancing 
high communication costs and sensitivity to client 
participation issues, especially in resource-con-
strained IIoT environments. Other methods focus on 
detecting alignment between local and global model 
updates. Deng et al. [37] adopted a client selection 
model that automatically evaluates examines, and 
automatically assesses, and investigates the quali-
ties of clients, choosing the most suitable clients for 
collaborative projects. Researchers have been using 
the reinforcement learning approach to develop a 
framework for learning success that considers sev-
eral variables [38, 39]. Challenges remain, particu-
larly with clients lacking sufficient computational 
power, which can delay training. Lai et al. [40] pre-
sented FL structure prioritizes client engagement in 
global training by utilizing the most beneficial data 
in enhancing model precision and training speed. 
Xu et al. [41] presented Fedcs, an innovative FL 
method that establishes a time frame for uploading 
and updating local models. To enhance the training 
process, the server tried to collect as many client 
updates as possible within the time limit by using a 
greedy selection. Du et al. [42] created a selection 
technique to minimize model training duration by 
prioritizing clients with faster upload times. They 
also developed a scheduling method that reduces 
the iteration upload time and adjusts the number 
of iterations using the maximum remaining band-
width. Overall, effective client selection is essen-
tial for improving learning efficiency in real-world 
federated tasks.
Model Compression: Sketching and structured 
updates Compression approaches allow clients to 
submit smaller model updates to the FL server at 
the end of each round. Sparsification, probabilistic 
quantization, and subsampling have also been used to 
reduce communication costs. In [43–45], the authors 
used techniques like federated dropout and lossy 
compression to further minimize the cost of com-
munication from the server to the participant. The 
central aggregator manages the build-up of error and 
momentum. Recent studies have presented a hierar-
chical communication pattern strategy that reduces 
reliance on the central server. Edge servers gather 
updates from edge devices before sending them to 
the cloud servers.
To address this problem, Li et al. [46] presented a 
corset-based FL framework that analyzes redundancy 
in the dataset and achieves high accuracy with a com-
pact network. Additionally, an effective asynchronous 
FL technique in [47] is used in edge computing. This 
approach uses the client node to adaptively calcu-
late the threshold based on the parameter throughout 
each round of model training. Two communication-
efficient FL frameworks presented in [48], CS-FL and 
1-bit CS-FL, are based on the CS approach. In CS-FL, 
local updates are compressed using analog compres-
sion techniques, and these compressed updates are sent 
to the server. Sparse local updates are compressed into 
1-bit compressed measurements in 1-bit CS-FL. These 
methods help to efficiently reduce the amount of data 
transmitted during FL training, both in the uplink and 
downlink.
Most data compression techniques result in lossy 
compression and increased communication efficiency 
at the expense of accuracy [49], which can negatively 
impact model correctness to address this optimiza-
tion problem with multiple objectives [50, 51]. The 
Multi-Objective Evolutionary Algorithm (MOEA) 
[51–53], has been used for multiple-objective optimi-
zation. This technique helps in finding the best solu-
tion and has been used to optimize the topology of the 
neural network model [54], leading to a decrease in 
communication expenses and an improvement in the 
overall performance of the FL model. Furthermore, 
MOEA was also employed by Lan et al. [55] in skin 
cancer detection applications to ensure effective dis-
ease detection while protecting patient confidentiality.

II. Heterogeneity in Systems: Federated networks 
face several challenges due to the heterogeneity of IIoT 
participants in terms of diverse hardware capabilities, 
processing capacity, storage, and network connectivity. 
Differences in capabilities can lead to problems such as 
fault tolerance, delayed mitigation, and stragglers. To 
address these issues, various strategies have been pro-
posed, including fault tolerance, client participation, 
and asynchronous communication. Bonawitz et al. [63] 
introduced a method for selecting a subset of authorized 
devices from a cluster of devices. However, it is typically 
necessary to verify the device's power status, whether 
it is idle, and whether it is an active network. It is also 
necessary to consider scenarios in which the device is 
offline. Asynchronous communication is a feasible strat-
egy for mitigating stragglers in heterogeneous situations. 
Device variability increases the risk of stragglers in syn-
chronous techniques. Unfortunately, the bounded-delay 
assumptions used to limit the metric of staleness also 
affect asynchronous communication. Client participation 
schemes provide an additional means of managing vari-
ability. These schemes select participating devices based 
on data distribution, data quality, or system resources. 
For example, the authors extended the FedCS protocol 
in [64], and their hybrid-FL protocol considers the vari-
ations in the data distributions of the involved clients. 
The optimal distribution of resources needed for model 
training is also achieved through the application of deep 
Q-learning [62, 65–69]. The amount of data that clients 
provide, or use determines the extent of their participa-
tion. To effectively manage heterogeneous systems, it is 
necessary to handle heterogeneous devices and networks, 
encourage user participation, and create fault-tolerant 
solutions for unreliable networks. Table 3 summarizes 
the methods and techniques for handling heterogeneous 
systems.
III. Statistical Heterogeneity: The system and data used 
in statistical analysis can vary significantly, making pro-
cessing complex particularly with non-IID data. Local 
trained models outperform the globally shared model for 
certain clients, which can exclude them from participat-
ing in the federated network. This complexity is increased 
in FL, which typically uses stochastic gradient descent 
[70–73]. When the data is IID, the stochastic gradient 
is unbiased, but this is not the case with non-IID data.

federated averaging without assuming constraints has 
been used to demonstrate the convergence rate of the 
algorithm. Their findings demonstrate that even in the 
worst scenario, their algorithm is still able to achieve at 
least 50% accuracy, despite poor convergence. Li et al.

Moreover, multitasking learning approaches in [80] is uti-

can better reflect the unique preferences of each user.
IV. Privacy Concerns: While many studies assume that 
attackers have limited access to confidential data, real-
world scenarios often require users to upload private 
information for training, resulting in a loss of control 
over their data. Nevertheless, FL enhances privacy by 
providing local gradient information instead of raw data, 
transmitting this information can still expose user privacy 
to central servers or third parties. Sensitive information 
may be revealed by the models themselves, even if the 
service provider takes reasonable precautions to secure 
the user's original dataset.
A secure aggregation algorithm [63], works based on the 
sliding mode control (SMC) method seeking to protect 
the privacy of each client model by avoiding disclosing 
the personal information of partners who are not trusted. 
The algorithm works properly even if one-third of the 
clients choose not to participate in the aggregation, as 
it is fault-tolerant for up to one-third of users. One tech-
nique to infer user information from a model is through a 
model inverting attack [81], which establishes a connec-
tion by pretending that there is a connection between the 
unknown input and the expected output. Zhu et al. [82] 
suggested an algorithm that uses the aggregation gradient 
that every client receives back from the central server to 
retrieve the original image provided by the user.

2.3  FL: applications
FL is a method used in big data environments where mali-
cious attacks involve verifying the accuracy of the infor-
mation transmitted by clients and improving this accuracy 
in each round based on the information provided. Moreo-
ver, edge servers or mobile smart devices may capture 
users'behavioral patterns and personal information. FL has 
made significant contributions to a variety of industries 
thanks to the collaborative efforts of numerous academics 
such as smart cities, finance, healthcare, industry, and urban 
services [94]. By leveraging FL, you can create intelligent 
IIoT systems that learn from data across multiple sources 
while preserving privacy and security. Major industry play-
ers, including Google, Apple, and Microsoft, have already 
embraced and implemented FL into their operations. For 
example, Google and Apple have used FL to improve the 
accuracy of their keyboard apps. Similarly, Microsoft 
applied a training model to forecast the chance of getting 
infected with malware while running Windows on a com-
puter. The main applications of FL are shown in Fig. 6. The 
use of FL in these well-known scenarios will be addressed 
in detail in this section.
I. Smart city: Collaboration between government agen-
cies, private enterprises, and individuals is essential for 
the development of a city [70, 71]. However, with stricter 
data privacy regulations, third-party access to data from 
data centers is limited [72, 73], resulting in decreased 
data exchange. Data isolation has been addressed by FL, 
which has integrated data at all city levels and enhanced 
urban applications and transit services for residents [95, 
96]. Governmental and commercial organizations are the 
data owners (clients) in the context of smart cities, while 
the urban data management center provides services. The 
service provider collaborates with city institutions to train 
a global model and enhance the quality of urban services 
offered to residents to improve smart city construction.
In [97] their work provided a detailed account of the 
potential of FL in smart city insight. They also identi-
fied the released issues and limitations in its application, 
intending to guide scholars in this field. Meanwhile, a 
spatiotemporal prediction technology was developed 
which combined FL to protect data privacy while ensur-
ing high prediction accuracy in smart city construction 
[98]. Lastly, Yuan et al. [99] presented a federated DL 
algorithm that utilized spatiotemporal long-term and 
short-term networks to predict traffic flow in smart cit-
ies. The algorithm employed observed historical traffic 
data to guarantee data confidentiality and successfully 
alleviate traffic jamming.
FL presents a new approach to building smart cities. This 
method offers enhanced data privacy protection while 
also facilitating the distribution of data across the whole 
city. The FL technique encourages the growth of smart 
cities by utilizing the potential advantages of urban data, 
enabling citizens to fully benefit from high-quality urban 
services.
II. Finance: Collaboration across financial organizations 
has become the norm in the banking and insurance sec-
tors, intending to make the most of big data and realize 
its full potential [100]. In recent years, a few financial

[111]. Many researchers have explored ways to integrate

distributed matrix decomposition system is presented in

recommendation technique [113] combines matrix fac-

network resources and edge-side training rates for practi-

update based on the distribution of local data, thereby 
reducing computation and communication requirements

3  Threats and mitigation strategies
Protecting data privacy and integrity is an important aspect 
of security. However, privacy takes it one step further by 
safeguarding personal data. When dealing with sensitive 
data, privacy should be given more importance, whereas 
security mainly aims to prevent unauthorized access to data. 
In FL, the protection of the global federated model and the 
local model is at risk due to various attack techniques. This 
section covers the use of blockchain technology as a decen-
tralized security method, and the two most studied attack 
types in FL: poisoning and Byzantine attacks. Furthermore, 
in this section, we will review previous research on the men-
tioned attack techniques to gain insight into the current state 
of FL security defense mechanisms.
3.1  Blockchain and FL security
Numerous research studies have been conducted to explore 
the potential advantages and obstacles of merging these two 
technologies. The aim is to develop a secure framework that 
ensures secure and private data sharing in IIoT by integrating 
FL and blockchain [130]. This combination facilitates secure 
and confidential sharing and analysis of data. Although 
blockchain technology can help address many challenges 
inherent in distributed ML environments, such as security, 
transparency, and decentralization, it is crucial to consider 
the potential obstacles and trade-offs [131]. These could 
include high computational cost, storage requirements and 
scalability issues related to traditional blockchains having 
low transaction throughput, which can delay FL aggrega-
tion processes and impact real-time IIoT applications [132]. 
However, when integrated correctly with FL, blockchain-
optimized consensus mechanisms like Proof of Stake (PoS) 
and Practical Byzantine Fault Tolerance (PBFT) [133], it 
can significantly improve the overall efficiency and effective-
ness of the system. PoS is a lightweight consensus mecha-
nism that selects validators based on their stake, reducing 
the need for energy-intensive computations like in Proof of 
Work (PoW). PBFT is well-suited for secure and reliable 
systems but can suffer from high communication overhead in 
large-scale networks. Lightweight Blockchain structures like 
sharding, pruning, and off-chain storage are used to mini-
mize storage burdens on IIoT nodes. Furthermore, hybrid 
Blockchain architectures are presented to balance decen-
tralization with efficiency for scalable FL implementation. 
By addressing these challenges, blockchain can enhance 
data integrity, security, and transparency in FL-based IIoT 
systems while maintaining efficiency [134]. Below are the 
primary types of FL attacks, where blockchain technology 
solutions have been utilized to address challenges related to 
data poisoning and model poisoning in FL attacks, aiming to 
improve communication efficiency, implement synchroniza-
tion strategies, strengthen system robustness, and incorpo-
rate privacy-preserving techniques.
3.2  Major FL attack types
	
I.	 Poisoning Attacks: FL is a process where numer-
ous clients collaborate to train the ML model without 
exposing sensitive data. However, this process is vul-
nerable to poisoning attacks that aim to manipulate, 
disrupt, or contaminate the local training dataset/
models through the training process. These attacks 
compromise the security of the FL system, as men-
tioned in [83]. Both model poisoning and data poi-
soning are primary types of poisoning threats that 
attack FL frameworks.
a.	 Data Poisoning Attacks: in data poisoning attacks, 
attackers deliberately alter the source tags or proper-
ties of local client data to affect the training results 
of federated models [135]. Attackers can interfere 
with the data-gathering process, making it difficult 
to identify FL clients without directly jeopardizing 
the FL-trained model. In recent years, defensive 
tactics have been developed to counteract data poi-
soning attacks. Some of these techniques remove 
outliers by determining the similarity of the data. 
The flowchart shown in Fig. 7 illustrates the spe-
cific steps of data poisoning attacks, from generat-
ing malicious data to impacting the global model. 
To protect against data poisoning attempts in FL, 
Tian et al. suggested a method to identify and sup-
press probable outliers [86]. Qi et al. created an FL 
framework that includes consortium blockchain 
approaches for traffic flow prediction using FL. This 
platform stores and verifies models trained from dis-
persed cars on the blockchain to avoid data poison-
ing attempts. Additionally, a Differential Privacy 
(DP) approach with noise addition procedures is 
used to improve data security within the FL frame-
work [87, 88]
b.	 Model Poisoning Attacks: model poisoning 
attacks refer to the insertion of a backdoor attack 
by malicious users into the global federated model 
or the local client model, resulting in the model 
generating particular incorrect outputs. These 
attacks are more effective than training data poi-

a significant concern in FL, where the focus is often 
on incentivizing clients with sufficient data quality 
to participate in the learning process while neglect-
ing the issue of malicious client attacks. Poisoning 
attacks typically involve single-user or server attacks, 
but Byzantine attacks involve collusion among multi-
ple users within a distributed learning environment. 
In FL, a malevolent attacker might exert influence 
over numerous clients, referred to as Byzantine users, 
who may upload fraudulent data because of faulty 
hardware, erratic communication routes, or inten-
tional fraud, breaking FL's convergence and jeopard-
izing the global model [91].
On the way to enhance the defense against Byzantine 
attacks, researchers have explored various approaches 
and strategies. For instance, they proposed a credibility-
based method in [92] to defend against Byzantine attacks 
which aims to evaluate the accuracy of the transmit-

improve the detection of such attacks with distributed 
data that are non-identical and non-independent (non-
IID), Zhai et al. [91] developed a Byzantine robust model 
for FL. Their approach included the integration of an 
adaptive anomaly detection model and transfer learning 
[136]. Similarly, Li et al. [93] introduced a secure block-
chain FL framework resisting Byzantine attacks. This 
method uses Byzantine consistency validation and vali-
dators to run parallel intensive validation procedures to 
detect attackers and improve the efficiency of model ver-
ification. Differential privacy and homomorphic encryp-
tion techniques enhance model security while preserv-

4  Opportunities, future trends, 
and implications
Currently, AI's rapid development is accelerating the intel-
ligent digitization process across many industries. However, 
this progress raises concerns about data fragmentation and 
data islanding [137, 138], limiting the potential value of data 
and making it difficult for different fields to share data. A 
solution to these issues has been found in the FL and has 
garnered attention from numerous academics. However, 
many obstacles remain in the way of FL development, and 
no single approach can fully address the challenges that arise 
with the use of FL technology in real-world applications. 
One critical area that requires investigation is the devel-
opment of more effective defensive attack strategies and 
encryption algorithms to enhance FL security. Criminals 
are increasingly using sophisticated methods to steal user 
data, including computer viruses, DOS, and DDOS attacks 
[139], which poses a risk to the privacy of user information.
	
I.	 To improve FL's security and protect against a 
broader range of attack threats, more advanced 
encryption and attack detection techniques must 
be developed [140]. The introduction of new com-
puter viruses and DOS and DDOS attacks poses a 
greater risk of revealing private user information, 
which hinders data sharing across participating 
firms in FL. Also, integrating FL with other secu-
rity methodologies, such as blockchain, could be 
a successful strategy to guarantee cross-domain 
learning security. Data from external sources can 
help service providers identify and stop attacks 
and create secure and efficient defensive plans 
[141].
	 II.	 Due to increased demands on processing capacity and 
inter-device communication capabilities, it is neces-
sary to optimize the communication costs between 
clients and servers. Currently, many communica-
tions are required for the global model to converge, 
which is not always feasible due to network band-
width, regional economy, and other factors [142]. 
Also, the traditional FL mechanism ignores differ-
ences among participants and the incentive structure 
of the cooperative system, making it difficult for new 
members to join the system. To address these con-
cerns, researchers are designing more efficient and 
fair FL algorithms. However, there isn't a universal 
FL method that works for all real-world applications. 
Therefore, specific demands and resource limitations 
must be considered while adjusting the optimization 
objectives and training techniques. The federated

5  Conclusion
The FL technique has gained significant attention and rapid 
development recently as a primary solution to preserve 
data privacy and security. This technique has several criti-
cal characteristics, including existing aggregation methods 
and strategies for addressing issues such as communication 
costs, heterogeneity, and data confidentiality. Demonstrat-
ing these aggregating methods establishes the groundwork 
for comprehending FL's capabilities. Categorizing and dis-
cussing techniques for dealing with communication costs, 
heterogeneity issues, and data confidentiality are critical for 
guaranteeing effective and secure FL deployments.
The integration of IIoT and FL is a significant point 
that is discussed in this survey. This integration has enor-
mous potential for developing intelligent industrial sys-
tems. Industrial systems can benefit from increased intel-
ligence, predictive maintenance, and optimized operations 
by merging IIoT sensor data with FL's distributed learn-
ing capabilities. This integration allows for real-time data 
analysis, collaborative learning, and decision-making at 
the edge, resulting in more efficient and smarter industrial 
operations. One of FL's significant features is its ability to 
provide localized model training on edge devices while 
maintaining data privacy. FL enables edge devices to par-
ticipate in model training without communicating their 
data to centralized servers, hence protecting data privacy, 
and mitigating the risks of data breaches. This decentral-
ized approach allows edge devices to contribute knowledge 
while keeping control of their sensitive data.
Another significant point discussed in this survey is 
security and privacy. FL security is an important issue 
that demands thorough examination and analysis. Detailed 
and thorough findings on FL security serve to close gaps 
in the existing literature and contribute to a better knowl-
edge of potential vulnerabilities and mitigation measures. 
By addressing security concerns, FL can acquire broader 
adoption and deployment across multiple domains. A 
detailed analysis and evaluation of recent FL studies yields 
significant insights into the field's accomplishments and 
problems. By reviewing the most recent research, prac-
titioners and researchers can acquire a thorough grasp of 
the state-of-the-art in FL and propose areas for further 
investigation and development.
Finally, investigating the integration of FL with other 
technologies such as blockchain, federated reinforcement 
learning, and federated meta-learning offers exciting per-
spectives for future advancements. By combining FL with 
these technologies, new opportunities arise for enhanced 
privacy, scalability, and collaboration in distributed learn-
ing systems. Understanding the current improvements and 
indicating the future directions and emerging trends in FL 
is crucial for shaping the development and adoption of this 
transformative strategy.

Abstract: The Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) applications have been recognized as an advancement of the conventional wireless network that concentrates on incorporating processes and machines specifically for industrial applications. These Industrial applications frequently use centralized machine learning (ML) approaches not only to enhance their functionality but also to evaluate sensor data for a variety of purposes, including digitizing operations in manufacturers, forecasting maintenance requirements in industrial equipment, and detecting anomalies for security monitoring, they may adversely affect overall system performance due to high cost of computing power and privacy concerns, as so much data is stored on a cloud server. Federated Learning (FL) has emerged as a new benchmark for centralized ML methods. It sends models to user devices without transferring private data to third-party or central servers; it is one of the promising solutions to data leakage issues. This work introduces a comprehensive overview of the advancements, challenges, and future directions in FL adoption with edge devices. It covers security threats and mitigation strategies, emphasizing its categories, privacy and concerns, communication overhead obstacles, heterogeneity issues, aggrega- tion techniques, and associated development tools. This review paper delves into FL-related topics, including system platforms, offering a comprehensive overview of best practice systems in real-world FL applications. To ensure security in IIoT applications, reviewing threats and mitigation strategies by integrating FL with state-of-the-art technologies such as blockchain, federated reinforcement learning, and federated meta-learning has been explored. Finally, the recent research is taking place to determine new future directions and opportunities for FL security defense mechanisms has been considered at the end of this review paper.
